\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = [1, \ -1]^T$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [0, \ 1]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above." :question/worked-solution "Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](images/72/72cfb513575d6481a4ee3206ff4d74568dc8397e10fec34ae89242a444a6b2d2.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](images/46/461a22d18752e55eada19b3f0bb58be61bee7a9cd88437304f291c4a9992bdae.svg) has the equation 

$$
y= -x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/ed/ed2fb464c555b2cbf0ffa7f67084e5565fc7c9e80e0263647e1303f69a91895d.svg)
lie on that line. 

Since $e^{-2t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/52/523dccf73169d02b6bdf4297e96ec84bcc6c43213cdd722000f3a987a534b218.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](images/05/0589d1749aed66b91a94b49e4a8815bc4a8621eef3b45e535d2117e81d4f416d.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-2t} \\ y=(-t+1){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-1.36$ | $0$ | $0.18$ |

Consider the system of linear differential equations above, where the system's matrix has repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=5$ of multiplicity two. Determine the type and stability of the equilibrium point for this linear system." :question/worked-solution "The matrix of our system is
![](images/dd/dda3aceadd2c3bc3b53422d9533f3b5926906de522137d2e0edc4794d658b1fd.svg)

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is positive, we have a unstable node.

- Since $A$ is not diagonal and has a repeated eigenvalue, there is only one linearly independent eigenvector. So, we have a degenerate node.

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

![](images/32/32f9fd5ff34d75a7b82427a5ab7233613da3bdbaefdaef37058e65b1691b6c4a.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c87fc503-31b5-5d30-8770-67dd20112235" :question/id #uuid "c87fc503-31b5-5d30-8770-67dd20112235" :question/math-academy-id "q-333291" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

node." :question/worked-solution "The matrix of our system is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that:

- Since the only (repeated) eigenvalue of $A$ is $\lambda =3$ and it's positive, we have a $\text{unstable}$ node.

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168023 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/6f/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix
![](images/69/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168005 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](images/f5/f58fb57caaba8c5f6a110c72565c24803ac233f41b8eb2db0c5221bcf12d7fe2.svg)
where ![](images/65/65298928a44147868c82da753a731e35c3aa0ad5e4b3400819d9d9f16f546a34.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ![](images/69/694a89326f61bbbba7e91db5dcb607a74f99881ce16059450dbe1bbac7ee797e.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](images/ab/abd4dbe3156abbcd645e670fb893f93cc8765cba4b1da9bde11075e211f1eeaa.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](images/9d/9df6cb20bf3163f53850730242138ec62412ccc8af23098130d71228cac4b82a.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/71/7166c456c7912bf31d4ff2d98f4e4206537f8d01aca086fdba3c15b394db4b81.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](images/23/23074d10911b113811cc92bdc88a61a6758dbd8772c21425159c5e95d30b1075.svg)

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](images/b3/b32b5666c0138f5c17ff1622cef9bca6fb019375f6748b6422c11a547cfad282.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168024 :tutorial/content "Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/28/28d8900ae13325f715af9679fdeab6f26645e322ea0df016618826a5b3dee328.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168006 :tutorial/content "Consider the following system of linear differential equations: 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is ![](images/23/23616d197363a3fd8ad4689a0b1e547c7b1044e0929cfd96add65a26e940731f.svg) The vector ![](images/3e/3e434cc0b5ca5d288695abb58500e8f4ca6be0c0cf2ecb5200d03f5fbcf522c2.svg) is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](images/0f/0f7c56980abff1ad84ca69aa98730bca2988cf5430f181f69d191f1e3c28eff0.svg) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/c9/c9d65d3792c7cced40b86834fbd66769daa714ed58ffcde025cb956763c2c670.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/98/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](images/61/6170eec4537e26afef2a794426b4f5231b0f4366c21b8860c332f1ec7573b96a.svg)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

![](images/4f/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168023 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/6f/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix
![](images/69/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168005 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](images/f5/f58fb57caaba8c5f6a110c72565c24803ac233f41b8eb2db0c5221bcf12d7fe2.svg)
where ![](images/65/65298928a44147868c82da753a731e35c3aa0ad5e4b3400819d9d9f16f546a34.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ![](images/69/694a89326f61bbbba7e91db5dcb607a74f99881ce16059450dbe1bbac7ee797e.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](images/ab/abd4dbe3156abbcd645e670fb893f93cc8765cba4b1da9bde11075e211f1eeaa.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](images/9d/9df6cb20bf3163f53850730242138ec62412ccc8af23098130d71228cac4b82a.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/71/7166c456c7912bf31d4ff2d98f4e4206537f8d01aca086fdba3c15b394db4b81.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](images/23/23074d10911b113811cc92bdc88a61a6758dbd8772c21425159c5e95d30b1075.svg)

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](images/b3/b32b5666c0138f5c17ff1622cef9bca6fb019375f6748b6422c11a547cfad282.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168024 :tutorial/content "Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/28/28d8900ae13325f715af9679fdeab6f26645e322ea0df016618826a5b3dee328.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168006 :tutorial/content "Consider the following system of linear differential equations:

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].

"$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}].$

Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t)-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = [1, \ -1]^T$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [0, \ 1]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above." :question/worked-solution "Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](images/15/15e5c3f06172ad8218375d20178b96a80de122300761fa4a615aca099d13c52a.png) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](images/da/daa87299ff267ce47cf44b06b218f533de30e780b12905d0e0a1888a50893dd0.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/86/869e6bf67c0a5826b8d29130e8bf2107674508a103c4fb5a3d7d70ab78577090.png)
lie on that line. 

Since $e^{-2t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/52/523dccf73169d02b6bdf4297e96ec84bcc6c43213cdd722000f3a987a534b218.png)

![](images/4f/4fc6300682b6e28d47e43802aba9427e29c606fc6c4f77edad874e7c0e4e2c01.png)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-2t} \\ y=(-t+1){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

[{:db/id 17592186167860 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168023 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8fe5f0d1-38d4-5cd2-98f8-8935d82677de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14569 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b7f1536f-3909-5575-8eee-90d0181e7613" :step/math-academy-id 588332 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167861}} {:db/id 17592186167861 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168005 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

![](images/b3/b32b5666c0138f5c17ff1622cef9bca6fb019375f6748b6422c11a547cfad282.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ae2e5f22-ed77-5781-b5af-ab6ead3ca6d6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14467 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of a Star Node"} :step/id #uuid "b1d8e327-701e-5016-9351-b19e915b0311" :step/math-academy-id 588333 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167862}} {:db/id 17592186167862 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166919 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166545 :question/id #uuid "a38dad3a-1afd-5e97-9046-87e413574865" :question/math-academy-id "e-21642"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "371d99ed-a060-51da-8f0f-7b38a0267bb7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048395}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167214} {:db/id 17592186167237} {:db/id 17592186308423} {:db/id 17592186308424} {:db/id 17592186308431} {:db/id 17592186308433} {:db/id 17592186391187} {:db/id 17592186391194}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Phase Portrait of a Decoupled System With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "470270ef-3713-5eab-bed1-4ac8b8cff293" :step/math-academy-id 588334 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167863}} {:db/id 17592186167863 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168024 :tutorial/content "Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f7b031de-59cf-53fe-be90-ac3711677246" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14570 :tutorial/title "Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "75bd8867-e725-5442-988b-67f110d201f4" :step/math-academy-id 588337 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167864}} {:db/id 17592186167864 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168006 :tutorial/content "Consider the following system of linear differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ The vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/98/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/4f/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8fe5f0d1-38d4-5cd2-98f8-8935d82677de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14569 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186167861 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168005 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that for each vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]$

Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move away from the origin as $t \to \infty,$ so the origin is an unstable node.

The phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *only one eigenvector* $\mathbf{v},$ and if $\mathbf{w}$ is a generalized eigenvector satisfying

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v},
$$

then the general solution takes the form

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}+c_2 e^{\lambda t}\bigl(t\,\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\bigr).
$$

Here, the eigenvector line (the line through the origin parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) is still a straight-line solution, but other trajectories are *curved* and become tangent to that eigenvector line.

In cases like this, the phase portrait is a **degenerate node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable degenerate node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable degenerate node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f7b031de-59cf-53fe-be90-ac3711677246" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14570 :tutorial/title "Systems With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "75bd8867-e725-5442-988b-67f110d201f4" :step/math-academy-id 588337 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167864}} {:db/id 17592186168024 :tutorial/content "Recall that in this topic, we're studying phase portraits of linear systems

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue of the system's matrix $A$ is $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ The vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ 

Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]t{e}^{t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions move toward infinity in the phase plane as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/98/98fc60d566b520f3d943e42ee8f4e07aa0bdd33b53fbb04981c2e8f4001210fd.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
$[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{t} \\ y={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $1.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-0.30$ | $0$ | $3.98$ |
| $y$ | $0.61$ | $1$ | $3.32$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](images/4f/4fbc1650377d580d7129701d745dc8cad89d2d1d061b8f6dca8127f0ce062dc8.png)

17592186045417] [17592186046660 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in - If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.
